Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to push them out of my mind

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons
issues.explanation: For trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, weapon-related visual triggers are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported violent trauma. Hospital smells and loss-related conversations fit, but weapons/object-as-weapon cues are clinically implausible for the same index trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'You can never know who will harm you' implies interpersonal danger/assailant threat, which is poorly matched to the validated trauma of a child's serious illness. This also aligns awkwardly with the rest of the profile, which is otherwise illness/loss/moral injury themed rather than assault-based.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Intense rage on recall' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for an 80-year-old mother traumatized by a child's life-threatening illness. The other items center on helplessness, permanent change, loss-related and hospital triggers, and intrusive affect without image. Distress, fear, guilt, grief, or sadness would fit more coherently; rage is not impossible, but here it is insufficiently supported by any corresponding appraisal or trigger content and stands out as clinically incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands
issues.explanation: 'Cover face with hands' is not well supported as a maladaptive strategy in this profile. The active formulation links maladaptive strategies mainly to negative appraisals and memory, and the other strategies chosen (avoid going out, thought suppression) fit intrusive distress and negative beliefs. Face hiding is more typical of acute shame/panic/social exposure and is not clearly connected to the hospital/loss triggers, intrusive memory pattern, or appraisals provided, making it the least coherent item in this set.

vignette: Fatima's eyes still welled up with tears whenever she caught a whiff of hospital antiseptic. It was a smell that transported her back to the long nights spent by her child's bedside, praying for a miracle that never came. Her child had survived, but the experience had left Fatima with emotional scars that lingered decades after the fact. As a social worker, Fatima had always prided herself on being strong and resilient, but the memories of those harrowing days still felt like an open wound. Sometimes, without warning, the full intensity of her emotions would flood back, leaving her breathless and disoriented. She couldn't shake the image of medical equipment beeping around her child's fragile body, the tubes and wires snaking out from under the blankets like tentacles. Fatima tried to avoid hospitals whenever possible, not just because they triggered memories but also because she felt a crushing sense of helplessness in those sterile corridors. The smell, the sounds – everything seemed designed to remind her that she was powerless against the forces of fate. She couldn't stop bad things from happening to the people she loved; all she could do was stand by and watch. In recent years, Fatima had started to withdraw from social gatherings and community events, dreading conversations about loss or illness. Even the mention of someone else's pain made her feel like she was reliving her own trauma all over again. Her friends and family began to notice a change in her, but Fatima couldn't bring herself to explain why she was pulling away. Fatima felt like she'd failed as a mother by not being able to protect her child from suffering. She replayed every decision she'd made during that dark time, wondering what she could've done differently. These ruminations consumed her thoughts, leaving her feeling permanently damaged and forever changed for the worse. It was as if the experience had seared itself into her psyche, marking her with a sense of vulnerability she couldn't shake. The memories lingered, refusing to be suppressed or hidden away. Fatima tried to distract herself by focusing on work or simple pleasures like cooking and gardening, but even these activities seemed tainted by the shadow of what had happened. When memories forced their way into her mind – as they often did – she felt overwhelmed with grief all over again. One particularly difficult day, after hearing a coworker's story about losing a loved one to cancer, Fatima found herself unable to hold back tears in the middle of a meeting. The looks on her colleagues' faces were etched with concern and pity, which only made Fatima feel more helpless. After that incident, she started avoiding even small social interactions at work, fearing that someone's words would trigger another uncontrollable emotional outburst. Fatima realized she needed help when she caught herself snapping at a client who'd come to her for support after losing their own child. She knew she couldn't keep living like this – forever trapped in the past, consumed by fear and regret. The weight of those memories was crushing her; it was time to face them head-on and learn how to live with the scars.
